brief.head: Save for a rainy year
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s rule for fis­cal pol­icy: run a small pri­mary bal­ance every year and be non-discretionary, sav­ing room for large deficits in a 2008-style cri­sis or pan­demic. {041-C05}

brief.head: Money from thin air
brief.text: A cen­tral bank makes money out of thin air, Ajay Shah said, “just like the Bitcoin and Ethereum folk do”. It then sets the overnight in­ter­est rate[[x3]]. {041-J09}

brief.head: Friends who differ
brief.text: Hayek’s great rival was Keynes[[x4]], yet the bi­og­ra­pher of both found Hayek per­son­ally closer to Keynes than to his ally Friedman. Amit Varma loves that friends can dis­agree. {041-S05}

brief.head: Shaped by war and flu
brief.text: Friedrich Hayek fought in the First World War, where an at­tack in 1917 dam­aged part of the hear­ing in his left ear. In 1918 he sur­vived the Spanish flu. {041-S03}

brief.head: Nobody designed it
brief.text: Languages evolve with no cen­tral com­mit­tee[[x5]][[x6]], and nat­u­ral se­lec­tion made hu­mans and trees with no plan­ner, Amit Varma said. “There’s no God, though that is the sub­ject for an­other day.” {041-J10}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the papers that shaped them
lead.head: Small print, big ideas

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 41

body: People think of pa­pers as bor­ing, Amit Varma said at the start of the episode. He and Ajay Shah set out to prove oth­er­wise, with pa­pers they con­sider sem­i­nal, thrilling and well writ­ten, and which, Varma said, crafted the mod­ern world.
They promised five. They de­liv­ered four, three pa­pers and an essay, and Varma later ex­plained the short­fall: “Because the light is going down.” {041-J05}
Two picks were Shah’s and two Varma’s, run­ning from a French essay of the mid­dle[[x1]] of the nine­teenth cen­tury to an American speech of 1968.
## The read­ing list
Shah began with Milton Friedman’s *The Role of Monetary Policy*, which ap­peared in 1968. {041-R01}

Of the thou­sands of macro­eco­nomics pa­pers he has read, he said, this is the one that lights up the jour­ney of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury. It treats peo­ple as op­ti­mis­ers who re­spond to gov­ern­ment, and keeps mon­e­tary pol­icy to one mod­est job: sta­ble prices.
Varma fol­lowed with Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, which, ad­mit­ting his bias, he called the great­est work of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury. {041-R02}
Its ar­gu­ment is that knowl­edge is scat­tered across mil­lions of peo­ple and changes all the time, so no plan­ner can ever gather it. Prices do the co­or­di­nat­ing in­stead.

Shah’s sec­ond pick was Ronald Coase’s 1937 ar­ti­cle *The Nature of the Firm*. It asks why the econ­omy runs on bar­gain­ing out­side firms and on obe­di­ence in­side them, and an­swers that con­tract­ing is costly.

Varma closed with Frédéric Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen*, which gave his pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, its name. Its bro­ken win­dow, he said, taught op­por­tu­nity cost about sixty years be­fore the term was coined.
## Against the all-knowing
A dis­trust of the all-knowing ran through the con­ver­sa­tion.
Shah de­scribed the Keynesian par­a­digm that Friedman over­turned as one in which the pol­i­cy­mak­ers “are wise and all-knowing” and the peo­ple “are more or less dumb”.
Varma saw a sim­i­lar con­ceit in peo­ple drunk on power, with their “en­gi­neer­ing mind­set that we can de­sign this”. A lot of the time, he said, the state just needs to get out of the way.
Even within com­pa­nies, Shah ar­gued, power works bet­ter dis­persed. The great firms are in­sti­tu­tions that out­last their chief ex­ec­u­tives.
Prices moved both hosts. “When you pause to think about it, we are moved to rap­ture,” Shah said.
## Ways of think­ing

What lasts, Varma ar­gued, is less any paper’s con­clu­sion than the frame of thought be­hind it. “I think every great paper of eco­nom­ics is teach­ing us how to think about life and live our lives bet­ter,” he said. {041-C15}

For new­com­ers, Shah rec­om­mended Tyler Cowen’s *GOAT* as an ideal start­ing point on Friedman, Hayek and Keynes. Varma rec­om­mended Marginal Revolution University, whose videos, he said, are ba­si­cally recorded PowerPoints.
Then Varma of­fered a final thought. Bastiat, Hayek and Friedman are no more, he said, but ideas are what shape civil­i­sa­tion.
“One day, Ajay and I will also be gone,” he said, be­fore won­der­ing why it had to be some­day: they could be gone now.
The next shot be­longed to a lit­tle girl host­ing a par­ody chan­nel, *Nothing Is Nothing*. Shah sus­pected she had been play­ing with them all along. {041-J11}

second.label: Wittgenstein
second.head: Not a Tractatus in sight
second.deck: Amit Varma on what the great philosopher wrote in the First World War trenches
body: Friedrich Hayek, Amit Varma said, was the sec­ond cousin of Ludwig Wittgenstein, and read *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus*, Wittgenstein’s great book, be­fore it was pub­lished. {041-R11} The two men served to­gether in the First World War.
Varma once came across Wittgenstein’s wartime di­aries on Twitter. You think of a great philoso­pher, he said, and won­der what he must be writ­ing about in the trenches. {041-S04}

The an­swer was want­ing sex. Varma ad­mit­ted the de­tour was “com­pletely un­re­lated” to Hayek’s paper, and re­turned to how Hayek got into Marxism at the London School of Economics be­fore a book by Ludwig von Mises made him a clas­si­cal lib­eral.

quote.text: And in the trenches, he is just ba­si­cally writ­ing about want­ing to mas­tur­bate and want­ing sex.

third.head: The outsider’s Nobel

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the outsider who won the Nobel

body: Ronald Coase was a law thinker[[x2]], not even an econ­o­mist, Ajay Shah said, and yet he won the Nobel Prize in Economics. {#coasenobel} Amit Varma cut in with the name of the show: “Everything is ev­ery­thing.”

Being an out­sider, Shah ar­gued, was an ad­van­tage. Coase did not take the economists’ vo­cab­u­lary and mod­el­ling strate­gies for granted. “He cu­ri­ously won­dered why does this make sense.” {041-S07}

His puz­zle sounded al­most naive. Outside a firm, com­merce runs on prices, bar­gains and con­tracts. Inside its bound­ary wall, no­body ne­go­ti­ates: there is an or­gan­i­sa­tion chart, and peo­ple fall in line.

His an­swer, in 1937, was that con­tract­ing is costly. {041-C10} Deals take time, ef­fort and emo­tional en­ergy, and once signed they keep need­ing rene­go­ti­a­tion as the world mis­be­haves. Inside a firm, the boss sim­ply says what to do.

box.title: The papers on the table
box.text: Three pa­pers and an essay: Friedman on mon­e­tary pol­icy (1968)[[x7]], Hayek on knowl­edge (1945), Coase on the firm (1937) and Bastiat on the seen and the un­seen. Ajay Shah calls Friedman’s the turn­ing point of twen­ti­eth-century macro­eco­nomics. {041-R01}

sections.label: The first paper
sections.head: The people are not dumb
sections.caption: Friedman and the natural rate
body: John Maynard Keynes, Ajay Shah said, prac­ti­cally in­vented macro­eco­nomics in the fires of the Great Depression. Before him, no­body mean­ing­fully treated an econ­omy as a unit of ob­ser­va­tion. {041-C01}

The Keynesian pack­age that fol­lowed let gov­ern­ment man­age the busi­ness cycle, largely through fis­cal pol­icy, and rel­e­gated mon­e­tary pol­icy to low im­por­tance. It did not take the peo­ple se­ri­ously, Shah said.
Through the 1960s the pack­age came apart. In 1968 Milton Friedman be­came pres­i­dent[[x8]] of the American Economic Association, which gave him a plat­form for a speech. {#aea}

His cen­tral move, Shah said, was to treat peo­ple as op­ti­mis­ers: when gov­ern­ment acts, they re­spond. “You can have some data set and you can fit a model, but you should not as­sume that those re­la­tion­ships are sta­ble.” {041-C02}
## A floor for un­em­ploy­ment
Friedman also set out the nat­u­ral rate of un­em­ploy­ment. Some peo­ple are al­ways switch­ing jobs, laid off or out of the labour force, so un­em­ploy­ment can never be driven to zero.

Monetary pol­icy, in his frame­work, should pre­serve the value of the cur­rency in a sta­ble and pre­dictable way, and not chase am­bi­tious goals. A good cen­tral bank, Shah said later, is a sim­ple util­ity that de­liv­ers an in­fla­tion tar­get and does noth­ing else.

~ Shah added a sec­ond pil­lar. Friedman’s study of the Great Depression showed that when the bank­ing sys­tem blows up, it can take the econ­omy down with it. Ben Bernanke worked out the de­tails, and was run­ning the Fed in 2008. {041-C06}

quote.text: There is some­thing below which it can’t re­ally go with­out driv­ing the in­fla­tion to hell.

sections.label: The second paper
sections.head: What the planner can’t know
sections.caption: Hayek and the knowledge problem
body: Friedrich Hayek’s essay came out in 1945[[x10]] as a re­but­tal to the econ­o­mist Oscar Lange[[x9]], who wanted a Central Pricing Board to set the price of ev­ery­thing. “CPB, lovely acro­nym,” Amit Varma noted. {041-J14}

Planners, Hayek ar­gued, treat run­ning an econ­omy as a prob­lem of logic: col­lect the data and apply the right rule. But knowl­edge is too dis­persed to col­lect. “Sometimes even I do not know what my de­sires will be to­mor­row,” Varma said. {041-C07}
He bor­rowed Ajay Shah’s ex­am­ple from their episode on power: on a cloudy day peo­ple switch off their air con­di­tion­ers, and use them more at night. No one can pre­dict such things.
## Order with­out or­ders

So how can some­one in Mumbai co­or­di­nate with a trader in Ludhiana or a farmer in Bengal? Through prices. An earth­quake dis­rupts a tin fac­tory; you never hear of it, but the price of tin rises, and you economise.
Had prices been one person’s in­ven­tion, Varma said, he would be ranked among the great­est thinkers in human his­tory. Shah agreed. “It is noth­ing less than mirac­u­lous.” {041-C08}
~ Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok, Varma noted, have a line that al­most sums up the essay: “a price is a sig­nal wrapped in an in­cen­tive”.

quote.text: a lot of beau­ti­ful things in the world are the prod­uct of human ac­tion, but not human de­sign.
quote.who: Adam Ferguson, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: The third paper
sections.head: Inside the firm, no haggling
sections.caption: why firms exist
body: Ajay Shah’s sec­ond paper was Ronald Coase’s 1937 ar­ti­cle *The Nature of the Firm*[[x11]]. {041-R03} It opened his mind, he said, to think­ing about the mar­ket econ­omy, treat­ing the firm not as a black box that max­imises profit but as a com­pli­cated, messy thing to be un­der­stood.

Picture the mar­ket as atomic in­di­vid­u­als, all bar­gain­ing and con­tract­ing, Shah said, with lit­tle fortresses of firms in­side it. Contracting is costly, so within the fortress the boss says do this, and no­body hag­gles over the price.
That is ef­fi­cient, but it gives up the flex­i­bil­ity of mar­kets. The op­ti­mal size of a firm is where the trade-offs bal­ance out.
## Firms after Coase

Amit Varma added that a firm’s au­toc­racy is no case for au­to­cratic rulers: you join vol­un­tar­ily, sign a con­tract and can leave. Calling cor­po­rate work mod­ern slav­ery, he said, gets it wrong. {041-C12}

As trans­ac­tion costs change, Shah said, the firm should be rethought[[x12]]. Open-source soft­ware lets loose coali­tions of in­di­vid­u­als make what com­pa­nies once made, with­out the bur­den of being in­side a firm.

~ Nor need a firm be Stalinist. A com­pany like Hindustan Lever has had many changes of chief ex­ec­u­tive with­out chang­ing its char­ac­ter, Shah said, be­cause power in­side it is dis­persed. {041-C11}

quote.text: And then the day the doc­u­ment is signed, the uni­verse starts mis­be­hav­ing and doing strange things.

sections.label: The essay
sections.head: Six francs and a missing shoe
sections.caption: the seen and the unseen
body: Frédéric Bastiat’s essay *That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen* is where Amit Varma got the name of his pod­cast. It be­gins with a stone through a win­dow[[x13]]. {041-R04}

Onlookers give their gyan: the bro­ken win­dow is good for the econ­omy[[x14]], since the glazier will get six francs and money is mov­ing. Bastiat, in Varma’s telling, bor­rows a phrase of Ajay Shah’s to reply: “Hey, Mr. Gas, keep quiet.” {041-J08}
What is seen is the glazier’s six francs. What is not seen is the shoe or the book the owner would have bought with them. {041-C13}
This, Varma said, is op­por­tu­nity cost, de­scribed about sixty years be­fore the term was coined. Bastiat ap­plied it to taxes, state spon­sor­ship of the arts and con­scrip­tion.
## One game of Candy Crush

Varma teaches the essay in his writ­ing course. You sit down to write, play one game of Candy Crush, and lose the hour. The dopamine hits are what is seen. “The op­por­tu­nity cost is that you made your fu­ture self stupid,” he said. {041-C14}
~ He also rec­om­mended Bastiat’s *The Candlemaker’s Petition*, in which can­dle­mak­ers ask the gov­ern­ment to block the sun, and *The Law*, which he called a mas­ter­piece.

quote.text: I look at Bastiat and I think that is a model pub­lic in­tel­lec­tual. That’s a Renaissance man.

portraits.caption: Frédéric Bastiat
portraits.credit: Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain

quote.text: What strikes me about this paper and all good eco­nomic work is the think­ing be­hind it, that these are foun­da­tional prin­ci­ples, this is a frame you bring, this is how you think about some­thing.

p3.title: Stories behind the papers
p3.deck: A speech, a dying vow, two lone warriors and a prize twice won

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the 1968 speech that reset macroeconomics
stories.head: The speech that called the 1970s
body: In the 1950s, Ajay Shah said, Keynesian econ­o­mists were con­fi­dent they had licked the busi­ness cycle. The gov­ern­ment would run big fis­cal pol­icy, man­age the ups and downs, and that would be that.
Through the 1960s, that con­fi­dence came apart. A very fa­mous Kennedy tax cut in 1964, backed by mod­els and fore­casts, was sup­posed to do cer­tain things, and it did not re­ally work. {#kennedy}

In 1968 Milton Friedman be­came pres­i­dent of the American Economic Association, and gave a speech. In it, Shah said, “he told a story”: what mon­e­tary pol­icy can do, what it can­not, and how to think about such ques­tions.
Para after para, Friedman played through how peo­ple would re­spond to gov­ern­ment. He set out the nat­u­ral rate of un­em­ploy­ment. And he wrote it in plain English.
Then the world obliged. For ten or fif­teen years after the speech, old-style macro pol­icy did not work very well, and the in­fla­tion of the sev­en­ties clicked with what he had said. {041-S01}

Robert Lucas and col­lab­o­ra­tors such as Tom Sargent and Ed Prescott then turned his ideas into sim­ple, clean mod­els that could be brought to the data. That, Shah said, has be­come “the en­tire ma­chin­ery of mod­ern eco­nom­ics”.

~ The trail ends in today’s cen­tral banks. All the sen­si­ble coun­tries now run in­fla­tion tar­gets, Shah said, and India got there in 2015, with a huge dif­fer­ence to the sta­bil­ity of its econ­omy. {#india2015}
stories.why: A clearly ar­gued idea, de­liv­ered just be­fore events bear it out, can re­di­rect a whole dis­ci­pline, and later its in­sti­tu­tions. Shah’s ver­dict: it was “a good speech at the right time and it came out right in hind­sight”.
stories.postscript: Friedman’s 1968 ver­sion was about money sup­ply. Central banks gave that up in the early 1980s and steer in­ter­est rates in­stead, Shah said. {041-J12}

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the life and death of a hero
stories.head: Principles to the last breath
body: Frédéric Bastiat, one of Amit Varma’s he­roes, was born in 1801 and died in 1850 at the age of 49. He was a great es­say­ist and, Varma thought, a mem­ber of par­lia­ment for some time. {#bastiatborn}
Bastiat did not stay at his desk. He trav­elled around pop­u­lar­is­ing his work, and on a book tour in the US, Varma said, he caught tu­ber­cu­lo­sis[[x15]]. {041-S08}

Realising he was dying, Bastiat said some­thing to the ef­fect that he would scream out his prin­ci­ples with all the power in his lungs till his dying breath. “Tuberculosis lungs, right?” Varma said. “So deeply mov­ing, but that’s the kind of man that he was.”
~ Varma mar­vels that Bastiat stated ideas that schol­ars for­malised only decades later, in sim­ple lan­guage that ab­so­lutely any­one could un­der­stand. “It blows my mind,” he said.
stories.why: Bastiat put ideas into plain words decades be­fore schol­ars for­malised them, and treated them as worth his last breath. People come and go, Varma said at the episode’s end; ideas shape civil­i­sa­tion. {041-C16}
stories.postscript: Varma first gave Bastiat’s birth year as 1799, then set­tled on 1801.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Bastiat’s dying vow

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a decade-long fight for inflation targeting
stories.head: Nonsense, shouted on cue
body: Amit Varma in­ter­rupted the episode for some be­hind-the-scenes footage, or BTS. Someone off cam­era was coaxed into shout­ing at Ajay Shah: “Inflation tar­get­ing is non­sense.” {041-J01}
“You see what Ajay has to kind of go through,” Varma told view­ers. Then he turned se­ri­ous. {041-S02}
Shah, Varma said, was one of a hand­ful of peo­ple fight­ing for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing a decade be­fore it hap­pened in India[[x16]]. He and K. P. Krishnan were “like lone war­riors in a sense”.

~ India adopted the regime in 2015. Shah said it has made a huge dif­fer­ence in sim­pli­fy­ing and sta­bil­is­ing the Indian econ­omy, and Varma pointed view­ers to his eight-hour episode with Krishnan[[x17]], which tells the story in de­tail. “So con­grat­u­la­tions for that,” he told Shah.
stories.why: Reforms that look ob­vi­ous in hind­sight often begin as lonely, mocked causes kept alive by a few. The cause here was a tar­get: four per cent in­fla­tion, with the RBI held ac­count­able for hit­ting it. {#target}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the lone warriors of inflation targeting

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the award named after his hero
stories.head: Twice blessed by Bastiat
body: There used to be a global prize[[x19]] for jour­nal­ism named after Frédéric Bastiat, Amit Varma said, given to writ­ers who pro­mote the free so­ci­ety. Varma won it twice, in 2007 and 2015[[x18]]. {041-S09}
The money was use­ful at the time, he said, and val­i­da­tion is al­ways nice. But it meant a lot to him for an­other rea­son: the man the prize was named after.

Bastiat, in Varma’s eyes, was a Renaissance man with in­ter­ests across ev­ery­thing and no cre­den­tial­ism. He had not been to a great uni­ver­sity and was not part of the sys­tem, an out­sider whose ideas went against con­ven­tional think­ing. “I just love the man so much,” Varma said.
~ He thinks Tim Harford is the only other per­son to have won it twice.
stories.why: Being claimed by a tra­di­tion you ad­mire can mean more than the money. Bastiat is Varma’s tem­plate for think­ing with­out cre­den­tials, and his essay gave Varma’s pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, its name. {041-J15}

quiz.q: In Bastiat’s parable of the broken window, what is seen and what is not?
quiz.a: The glazier’s six francs; un­seen is the shoe or book the owner for­goes.

quiz.q: What is the one thing a good central bank should do, in Ajay Shah’s view?
quiz.a: Control the short-term in­ter­est rate to de­liver a sta­ble, pre­dictable in­fla­tion tar­get.

quiz.q: Whose proposal for a Central Pricing Board was Hayek’s 1945 essay written to rebut?
quiz.a: The econ­o­mist Oscar Lange, whom Varma urged lis­ten­ers to ig­nore com­pletely.

quiz.q: Why do firms exist at all, according to Ronald Coase’s 1937 article?
quiz.a: Because con­tract­ing is costly: bar­gain­ing, lawyer­ing and rene­go­ti­a­tion all take time and ef­fort.

quiz.q: Which book turned the young Hayek from socialism into a classical liberal?
quiz.a: *Socialism*, by Ludwig von Mises, read after Hayek had drifted into Marxism at LSE.

quiz.q: Who stopped colleagues in university hallways to ask if they had read Hayek’s essay?
quiz.a: The econ­o­mist Armen Alchian: “Have you read this? You have to read this.”

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 41. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Frédéric Bastiat (Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Ludwig Wittgenstein (Moritz Nähr, public domain); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Ronald Coase (University of Chicago Law School, Attribution); Ludwig von Mises (Ludwig von Mises Institute, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: The paper Ajay sees as the turn­ing point of 20th-century macro­eco­nomics in ideas and pol­icy: it treats peo­ple as op­ti­mis­ers, in­tro­duces the nat­u­ral rate of un­em­ploy­ment and con­fines mon­e­tary pol­icy to keep­ing prices sta­ble, be­cause in­fla­tion adds noise to price sig­nals.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Nature of the Firm
shelf.creator: Ronald Coase
shelf.why: Coase’s an­swer to why firms exist when mar­kets can co­or­di­nate through prices: con­tract­ing is costly.

shelf.title: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s bro­ken-window para­ble, which teaches you to look past a policy’s vis­i­ble ef­fect to its un­seen costs and in­tro­duced op­por­tu­nity cost decades be­fore the term ex­isted.

shelf.title: The Candlemaker’s Petition
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s satire takes pro­tec­tion­ist logic se­ri­ously until it reaches ab­sur­dity; once you’ve laughed at it, you can’t take ‘save local businesses’ rhetoric at face value.

shelf.title: The Law
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s mid-19th-century mas­ter­piece on the re­la­tion­ship be­tween the state and so­ci­ety, which Amit says car­ries wis­dom in every para­graph and is a strik­ingly mod­ern lens on India.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson
shelf.creator: Henry Hazlitt
shelf.why: Hazlitt’s 1946 ‘col­lec­tion of light bulbs’ that uses the ba­sics of scarcity and in­cen­tives to clear up fal­la­cies about price con­trols, tar­iffs, in­fla­tion and gov­ern­ment spend­ing, teach­ing you to ask what the money would have done if left with con­sumers.

shelf.title: I, Pencil
shelf.creator: Leonard Read
shelf.why: A pen­cil nar­rates its own mak­ing from ma­te­ri­als and know-how scat­tered across many coun­tries, co­or­di­nated by prices with no one in charge.

shelf.title: The Road to Serfdom
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s clas­sic ar­gu­ment for free­dom against state plan­ning: cen­tral plan­ning and its au­thor­i­tar­i­an­ism lead to serf­dom.

shelf.title: Socialism: An Economic and Sociological Analysis
shelf.creator: Ludwig von Mises
shelf.why: This is the book that turned the young Hayek from demo­cratic so­cial­ism and Marxism into a clas­si­cal lib­eral.

shelf.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
shelf.creator: Ludwig Wittgenstein
shelf.why: Wittgenstein’s great book, whose line ‘whereof one can­not speak, thereof one must be silent’ Amit loves and uses to argue that any one lan­guage is in­ad­e­quate.

shelf.title: Keynes vs. Hayek rap battles (‘Fear the Boom and Bust’ and ‘Fight of the Century’)
shelf.creator: Russ Roberts
shelf.why: A rap bat­tle be­tween ac­tors play­ing Keynes and Hayek, with lyrics by EconTalk’s Russ Roberts, which the hosts rec­om­mend to­gether with its se­quel, Fight of the Century: a de­light­ful way into the clash be­tween the two dom­i­nant eco­nomic schools of the 20th cen­tury.

shelf.title: Tyler Cowen on the Lex Fridman Podcast
shelf.creator: Lex Fridman
shelf.why: In it Cowen picks ‘The Use of Knowledge in Society’ as one of the three works most im­por­tant to him and ex­plains why.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley finds the same bot­tom-up process, with no plan­ner or de­signer, be­hind nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, lan­guage, prices, cul­tural norms and com­mon law.

shelf.title: Matt Ridley on The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Matt Ridley, a com­pan­ion to his book, on how order emerges bot­tom-up with­out cen­tral de­sign, across bi­ol­ogy, cul­ture and mar­kets.

shelf.title: K. P. Krishnan on The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Ep. 34) and From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Ep. 37), Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: GOAT
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: It is a de­light to read and pulls to­gether the lives and ideas of the econ­o­mists the hosts love.

shelf.title: Modern Principles of Microeconomics
shelf.creator: Alex Tabarrok and Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: It con­tains the line ‘a price is a sig­nal wrapped in an incentive’, which Amit says al­most sums up Hayek’s essay.

shelf.title: Marginal Revolution University
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: Amit calls it the best way to un­der­stand con­cepts like the price sys­tem and op­por­tu­nity cost clearly.

shelf.title: Marginal Revolution (blog)
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: The blog Amit thinks has been the best in the world for 15 years: two econ­o­mists think­ing aloud in clear prose every day, a model for aca­demics and bet­ter sense-making than a newspaper’s eco­nom­ics pages.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: In a be­hind-the-scenes clip, Amit gets some­one off cam­era to shout ‘Inflation tar­get­ing is non­sense!’ at Ajay, the man who spent a decade fight­ing for it, then turns to the au­di­ence: ‘You see what Ajay has to go through.’

Amit’s pub­lic ser­vice an­nounce­ment: ‘When peo­ple think of Hayek, they think Salma Hayek. When peo­ple think of Lange, they think Jessica Lange. No, you do not need to think about those fig­ures.’ Think of Friedrich Hayek, and ig­nore Oscar Lange com­pletely.

After not­ing that Hayek was per­son­ally closer to his rival Keynes than to his ally Friedman, Amit says: ‘So the few times you and I dis­agree, Ajay Shah, I don’t worry about our friend­ship at all.’
Ajay notes that Coase was a law thinker, not even an econ­o­mist, yet won the Nobel Prize in Economics. Amit cuts in with the show’s title: ‘Everything is ev­ery­thing.’

On why the five promised pa­pers be­came four: ‘Because the light is going down.’ That re­minds Amit of Bastiat’s Candlemaker’s Petition, in which can­dle­mak­ers ask the gov­ern­ment to block the sun.
Shooting out­doors, Amit clar­i­fies that ‘in the show notes below’ means below the YouTube screen, ‘not below where I am sit­ting be­cause there is grass and there is fresh earth.’
On Bastiat’s ques­tion of how a plan­ner could feed Paris: ‘And where are we going to grow upma? Though I don’t think any­one in Paris has upma.’
Amit has Bastiat si­lence the bro­ken-window op­ti­mists by bor­row­ing a phrase of Ajay’s from an ear­lier episode: ‘Hey Mr. Gas, keep quiet.’
Ajay ex­plain­ing cen­tral banks: ‘A cen­tral bank in­vents money. Okay, it makes money out of thin air. Okay, just like the Bitcoin and Ethereum folk do.’
Amit, list­ing prod­ucts of nat­u­ral se­lec­tion: ‘There’s no plan­ner. There’s no God, though that is the sub­ject for an­other day.’

Amit half-remembers Friedman’s line ‘in­fla­tion is al­ways and ev­ery­where a mon­e­tary phe­nom­e­non.’ Ajay replies ‘It’s complicated’: Friedman was wrong to em­pha­size money sup­ply, which cen­tral banks gave up try­ing to con­trol in the early 1980s, though the rest of his phi­los­o­phy holds.
The 1964 Kennedy tax cut in the US, cited by Ajay as the mo­ment con­fi­dent Keynesian fore­cast­ing vis­i­bly failed to de­liver.
Oscar Lange’s pro­posal for a Central Pricing Board (‘CPB, lovely acronym’) to set the price of ev­ery­thing. Hayek’s 1945 essay was writ­ten to rebut it.
Amit’s pod­cast The Seen and the Unseen takes its name from Bastiat’s essay ‘That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen’.
